claims.text: The Cantor CoCrFeMnNi alloy is a single-phase FCC alloy.
The proposed initial alloy has been heat-treated to relieve residual stresses and produce a homogeneous microstructure.
Continuous sliding wear removes the protective passive oxide film from Cantor alloy.
Wear-induced plastic deformation dynamically refines the near-surface grains of Cantor alloy.
Wear-induced dynamic amorphization produces an ultrafine-grained near-surface layer.
The refined near-surface layer has increased grain-boundary density.
Increased grain-boundary density accelerates diffusion of alloying elements involved in passive-film formation.
Chromium in Cantor alloy forms a passive layer that is important to its corrosion resistance.
Cantor-alloy corrosion resistance depends on processing-induced microstructure and residual stress.
Accelerated diffusion through the refined layer causes faster reformation of the passive film after wear removes it.
Mixed metal-oxide surface films formed during shear can reduce wear in high-entropy alloys.
At room temperature, rapid passive-film reformation establishes a dynamic equilibrium with mechanical film removal.
At room temperature, coupled tribo-corrosion produces lower corrosion-current density than isolated wear or corrosion testing.
At room temperature, coupled tribo-corrosion produces lower wear rate and total material loss than isolated wear or corrosion testing.
Lowering the test temperature suppresses grain-boundary diffusion in the refined surface layer.
Suppressed grain-boundary diffusion slows repassivation and increases corrosion rate, wear loss, and total degradation.
With load, speed, and electrolyte held constant, differences between room-temperature and low-temperature tests are principally attributable to diffusion and repassivation kinetics.
Temperature-dependent frictional heating and chemical kinetics could independently affect the comparison and cause the prediction to fail.

contradictions.description: The mediator equates dynamic amorphization with formation of an ultrafine-grained layer, whereas the proposed mechanism requires a crystalline layer containing a high density of grain boundaries. An amorphous layer does not possess the grain-boundary network invoked by the diffusion mechanism.
